title: VPC sidecar egress orchestration — customer POC notes
context:
Customer: fintech startup evaluating Redwood Private (VPC) for latency-sensitive NLP features. They require strong egress controls (restricted internet access), per-tenant isolation, and observable, auditable outbound flows for compliance.
  Goal: Produce a pragmatic POC network pattern that balances operational simplicity with least-privilege egress, minimal changes to customer infra, and clear failure modes. These are working notes for the SE runbook and workshop follow-ups.
requirements:
- Per-tenant logical isolation for network egress decisions (not necessarily separate accounts).
  - Deny-by-default egress: only approved domains/IPs and cloud APIs allowed.
  - Support for model pulls from private registries (ECR/GCR) and S3-like stores.
  - TLS termination and inspection options: prefer end-to-end TLS for customer traffic; egress proxy will do SNI/hostname allow-lists, not full MITM unless requested.
  - Low added latency: target <10ms p99 overhead from egress path for typical requests.
  - Observability: VPC Flow Logs, proxy access logs, per-tenant audit trail.
  - Fail-open fallback (controlled): if egress proxy is unavailable, fallback to restricted NAT path with alerting.
proposed-pattern-summary: Introduce a lightweight egress "sidecar" layer deployed into the customer VPC as a set of highly available EC2/ASG or k8s DaemonSet proxies that perform outbound routing decisions. Traffic from Redwood-managed inference nodes is routed (via route table or ENI) to the sidecar cluster which handles DNS resolution, allow-listing, and optional TLS routing. For cloud API access (S3/ECR), use interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) where possible to keep traffic on the AWS backbone. For external HTTP(S) egress, use the sidecar proxy with well-defined allow-lists and a per-tenant ACL evaluator.
why-sidecar:
- Avoids cross-account VPC peering complexity for multi-tenant customers.
  - Gives fine-grained control per outbound flow with minimal network changes.
  - Easier to instrument (proxy access logs) vs trying to parse VPC Flow Logs for application-level allow-lists.
  - Controls third-party hostnames via SNI and ALPN without full TLS interception (preserves cert pinning when needed).
networking-components:
- Redwood inference subnets: private subnets hosting model servers.
  - Egress sidecar subnet(s): small subnets with ASG/DaemonSet, SGs open only from inference subnets.
  - NAT fallback subnet: NAT Gateway(s) configured with highly-restricted route table pointing to a dedicated NAT that only allows approved IP ranges (emergency path).
  - Route tables: route inference-to-sidecar via target ENI or via explicit route 0.0.0.0/0 -> sidecar ENI (if supported), otherwise configure proxy as default gateway for inference nodes.
  - Interface endpoints (AWS): S3, ECR, STS, KMS (if needed) to avoid public egress for cloud APIs.
  - Route53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints (if customer uses centralized DNS) for split-horizon host resolution.
dns-strategy:
- Use Route53 Resolver outbound endpoints to forward specific domains to customer-managed DNS where private hostnames exist.
  - Sidecar performs a DNS hygiene step: enforce a TTL floor, cache positive answers for brief windows to reduce latency, and validate that resolved IPs match expected prefix lists (defend against poisoned responses).
  - Split-horizon: internal domains (*.internal) resolve to private IPs via conditional forwarding; external hosts resolved via public resolver but only allowed if on allow-list.
egress-controls-and-policy-eval:
- Policy sources: central Redwood allow-lists + customer-supplied tenant allow-lists (CSV/ConfigMap). Policies include domain patterns, CIDR ranges, and service tags (e.g., aws:s3).
  - Evaluation order: local tenant policy overrides central deny/allow; global deny rules (e.g., known-malicious CIDRs) enforced first.
  - SNI-based allow-list for HTTPS; for non-SNI TLS (raw IP) require explicit CIDR allow.
  - For HTTP(s) where inspection is required by compliance, optionally enable MITM with customer-managed CA (explicit customer opt-in).
interface-endpoints-and-peering-consider:
- Prefer interface endpoints for S3/ECR where supported to keep traffic private.
  - If customer requires cross-account access patterns, prefer AWS PrivateLink over VPC peering to limit route table complexity and avoid full-mesh peering scaling issues.
  - Transit Gateway only recommended for customers with many VPCs and existing TGW investment; for simple POCs TGW adds cost/ops overhead.
security-groups-and-nacl-guidance:
- SGs: inference nodes -> allow outbound only to sidecar SG on specific ports (443/80/8443). Sidecar SG allows inbound from inference subnets only.
  - Sidecar egress SG: allow outbound to interface endpoints and permitted CIDRs; deny 0.0.0.0/0 unless explicitly required.
  - NACLs: optional stateless filters as defense-in-depth for known-bad IP ranges.
observability-and-audit:
- Required telemetry: VPC Flow Logs (to CloudWatch/Datadog), sidecar access logs (structured JSON), Route53 Resolver logs where available.
  - Tagging: every egress log line should include tenant_id, model_id, request_id where possible (inferred from request headers and attached ENI tags).
  - Metrics: sidecar latency histogram, allowed/blocked counters by tenant, DNS resolution errors, NAT-fallback counts.
failure-modes-and-fallbacks:
- Sidecar outage: route via NAT fallback after a brief cooldown; escalate to SRE and disable fallback if policy requires strict deny.
  - DNS poisoning: sidecar rejects responses not matching expected CIDR ranges and falls back to resolver via Route53 outbound or raises an alert.
  - Interface endpoint throttling: fall back to guarded NAT path and rate-limit requests to avoid cascading failures.
operational-playbook:
- Workshop steps: 1) Inventory required outbound endpoints and private hostnames; 2) Deploy sidecar in staging with permissive allow-list; 3) Run traffic replay and measure p99 latency; 4) Tighten allow-list progressively; 5) Enable interface endpoints and test private pulls.
  - Smoke tests: curl to public allow-list host, s3 ls to customer bucket via VPC endpoint, ECR docker pull, simulate DNS edge-case (split-horizon mismatch).
  - Rollback: switch route table to point to NAT fallback, scale sidecar to zero, and apply emergency policy to deny all external egress.
test-cases-and-acceptance:
- Latency: additional p99 overhead <=10ms for common hosts in region.
  - Correctness: blocked hosts return 403/connection-reset within 300ms for HTTP flows.
  - Resilience: single AZ sidecar failure should not increase blocked flows; cross-AZ failover tested by AZ kill.
  - Observability: every request shows tenant_id in logs and corresponds with VPC Flow Logs entry.
open-questions:
- Customer preference on MITM vs SNI allow-list; legal/compliance runbook required for TLS interception.
  - Will customer allow a shared sidecar cluster per VPC or do they want one per tenant? Cost vs compliance tradeoff.
  - Acceptable SLA for sidecar (target HA zones, sync time for policy propagation).
next-steps-and-action-items:
- [ ] Run combo smoke test in Redwood staging with simulated tenant policies (owner: Aria).
  - [ ] Draft customer-facing one-pager explaining sidecar tradeoffs and failure modes (owner: Mateo).
  - [ ] Prepare Terraform module for quick deployment (owner: Infrastructure SE).
  - [ ] Schedule a compliance call to confirm TLS interception constraints (owner: Solutions Eng).
notes:
- This pattern is intended for customers who want tight egress control without the overhead of multi-account peering. For customers with heavy cross-VPC traffic or existing TGW, adapt pattern to use PrivateLink + TGW.
  - Keep sidecar images minimal and audited (runtime in distroless), rotate keys via KMS, and store allow-lists in versioned storage (git + signed releases).
